topic: Why a popular exhibit is not the same as a useful one
grammarFocus: 学术论证的限定、因果、对比与证据范围
title: Why a popular exhibit is not the same as a useful one
instructions: 原创学术微训练；场景、机构与数值均为虚构模拟，不是事实报道或官方试题。先独立阅读答题，再用原句核对限定、比较与因果。短篇专项不能替代完整陌生测评。
passage:
A. The fictional Harbour Museum introduced a touch-screen exhibit about shipbuilding. Its software counted every screen activation. During the first month, the new exhibit received more activations than any other display. The manager called it the museum's most effective educational resource. The education team welcomed the interest but questioned the strength of that conclusion.

B. A screen activation was not necessarily a separate visitor. Children sometimes touched the opening screen repeatedly while waiting for the animation to begin. The display also stood beside the entrance, whereas the older exhibits were in a room upstairs. Its location and novelty could attract attention independently of what people learned. These factors did not make the count useless; they changed what it could reasonably indicate.

C. To investigate learning, the team invited visitors to explain how a wooden hull was assembled. Some could name the main stages immediately after using the display. However, a group interviewed before entering the museum already knew several stages. A later visitor's correct answer could therefore reflect prior knowledge rather than new learning. The team added a brief entry question and compared each participant's account before and after the visit.

D. Even this comparison had limits. Participants willing to answer twice might have been unusually interested in shipbuilding. The study also measured immediate recall, not whether the knowledge lasted. A small follow-up interview was proposed for the next month, with consent and no requirement to join. The team expected some missing responses and planned to state the number contacted as well as the number replying.

E. The revised report described reach, engagement and learning separately. A popular display could reach many people without changing their understanding very much. A quieter display might produce substantial learning for a smaller group. Rather than declaring a single winner, the museum used the findings to revise the slow opening animation and improve signs directing visitors upstairs. The evaluation became a source of practical changes instead of a competition between exhibits.
